title: One Client, One Server: The Process Topology of MCP

questions.question: What is the relationship between an MCP client and an MCP server?
options: A client can multiplex requests to any number of servers over one shared connection
A client and a server always run inside the same operating system process
A server pushes updates to every client that has ever connected to it before
Each client holds exactly one connection to exactly one server for its lifetime
questions.explanation: A client is scoped to a single connection and a single server; a host that needs to reach several servers embeds a separate client for each one it connects to.

questions.question: Why does a host embed more than one client when it needs to reach more than one server?
options: Because each client holds only one connection, so a new server needs its own client
Because the specification requires a full process restart before adding any new server
Because a server refuses a client that has previously connected to a different server
Because a single client can only send one JSON-RPC request in its whole lifetime
questions.explanation: A client's connection is one to one with a server, so reaching a second server means instantiating a second client inside the same host, not reusing the first connection.

questions.question: During the initialize handshake, what does a server return alongside the negotiated protocol version?
options: A list naming every other server the host happens to be connected to
A capabilities object describing which features, such as tools, that server supports
The complete source code of every tool handler the server has implemented
The operating system username of the account that launched the host process
questions.explanation: The initialize response pairs the protocol version with a capabilities object, so the client learns exactly which features, such as tools or resources, that particular server supports before calling anything.

questions.question: Why are an MCP host and an MCP server usually described as separate trust domains?
options: They must run on physically separate hardware located in different data centers
Trust domains describe billing boundaries rather than anything about process isolation
They are separate processes, and the server's output is not inherently trusted by the host
The server encrypts every message so the host cannot read its own requests
questions.explanation: Host and server are independent processes, often written by different parties, so content the server returns crosses a real boundary and is treated as untrusted input rather than as code the host already trusts.

questions.question: A client sends an initialize request declaring protocol version 2026-07-28, but the server only speaks 2025-01-01. What should happen?
options: The server silently upgrades itself to 2026-07-28 and proceeds as though nothing happened
The connection succeeds and the mismatch is only logged if debug mode is enabled
The host process terminates immediately without giving the client any chance to respond
The server returns a structured error describing the mismatch instead of a result
questions.explanation: A version mismatch is a negotiation failure the server reports as an ordinary JSON-RPC error carrying a code and a message, which lets the host decide what to do next instead of crashing.

questions.question: A host is connected to two servers, files and search, each exposing a different tool. How does it know which one to call for a given tool name?
options: It builds a directory mapping each discovered tool name to the server that declared it
It sends the same request to every connected server and keeps whichever reply arrives first
It always routes every tool call to whichever server happened to connect first
It asks the end user to type the exact server name before every single call
questions.explanation: Because each server declares its own tools during discovery, the host can build a directory from tool name to owning server and route a call to the connection that actually implements it.
